scenes.narration: They don’t tell you about the silence in the training manual. They talk about bear safety, trail maintenance, and how to handle a lost hiker, but they never mention the kind of quiet that feels like it’s holding its breath. I’ve been a ranger at Blackwood Ridge for six years now, and I’ve learned that the forest has a rhythm. Usually, it’s a hum of insects, the rustle of wind in the hemlocks, or the occasional crack of a dry branch. But tonight? Tonight, the woods were dead. Not just quiet, but aggressively still. Like the entire ecosystem had just walked out of the room.

scenes.narration: I was about three miles out from the northern trailhead, checking on a reported downed power line. My flashlight beam felt pathetic, a thin, yellow ribbon cutting into a darkness that seemed thicker than usual. I stepped over a rotted log, my boots crunching on damp needles, and that’s when I heard it. It wasn't a bird. It wasn't a coyote. It was a sound that didn't belong in nature. It was like a radio tuning between stations—static, muffled voices, and a high-pitched, oscillating frequency that made the fillings in my teeth ache.

title_and_description.title: I'm a Park Ranger, and I Found Something in the Woods That Shouldn't Exist
title_and_description.description: A harrowing, true-sounding account of a park ranger’s encounter with the creature known as Siren Head. Based on a chilling firsthand narrative from the deep woods of Blackwood Ridge.
